newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada auto union to issue key proposal by Monday.
newsitem.headline: Canada auto union to issue key proposal by Monday.

text.p: The Canadian Auto Workers (CAW) union said it will deliver the union's first key proposal to its 1996 strike target, Chrysler Canada Ltd, by Monday.

Union president Buzz Hargrove said negotiators are trying to craft a proposal that could form the basis of an agreement between the union and Chrysler Corp's wholly owned unit to set the pattern for the entire auto industry in Canada.
"We're trying to define more clearly in our own minds what we're trying to accomplish here and how you go about doing that," Hargrove said.
However, Hargrove was not certain the negotiations would bear fruit ahead of the strike date and said the thorny issue of outsourcing could prove to be a dealbreaker.

"I think it's fair to say they've accepted they're going to have to discuss it (outsourcing), but we haven't got them to the point where they're prepared to say they have to agree to something different than what they are doing," he said.

Chrysler spokesman, Walt McCall, noted the carmaker averted strikes in the last two negotiating rounds. He said it may have greater flexibility on outsourcing than Ford Motor Co or General Motors Corp.

"The last couple of times it hasn't been so much economic packages but whatever the current burning issue is and this year I guess its outsourcing, which isn't as big an issue with us as it is with the others," McCall told Reuters.

The CAW is Canada's largest private-sector union with about 52,800 auto workers out of a total membership of 210,000. It broke away from its American cousin, the United Auto Workers (UAW) union in 1985 in a dispute over profit sharing for workers, but retains close ties to the UAW.

Although contracting out work in the auto industry is a major issue at all three carmakers, General Motors Canada in particular has made outsourcing decisions in the last year that will eliminate over 5,000 CAW jobs.
The CAW last held a strike at Ford Canada for nine days in 1990.
